λmin​(Ax)​‖fθ​(x)Φ∗∗−y‖22≤‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,z)‖22≤λmax​(Ax)​‖fθ​(x)Φ∗∗−y‖22.\lambda_{\min}(A_{x})\bigl\|f_{\theta}(x)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}-y\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\leq\bigl\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\leq\lambda_{\max}(A_{x})\bigl\|f_{\theta}(x)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}-y\bigr\|_{2}^{2}. (76)

Under the condition λmin​(Ax)>0\lambda_{\min}(A_{x})>0, we rearrange these inequalities to get

‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,z)‖22λmax​(Ax)≤ℛΦ∘​(θ,z)≤‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,z)‖22λmin​(Ax).\frac{\bigl\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}}{\lambda_{\max}(A_{x})}\leq\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)\leq\frac{\bigl\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}}{\lambda_{\min}(A_{x})}. (77)

Since Φ\Phi is differentiable and strictly convex, its Hessian ∇2Φ​(fθ​(x)Φ∗)\nabla^{2}\Phi(f_{\theta}(x)_{\Phi}^{*}) is positive definite. The Fenchel–Young loss further admits the quadratic bound

λmin​(HΦ​(θ))​‖fθ​(x)Φ∗∗−y‖22≤ℛΦ​(θ,z)≤λmax​(HΦ​(θ))​‖fθ​(x)Φ∗∗−y‖22.\lambda_{\min}(H_{\Phi}(\theta))\bigl\|f_{\theta}(x)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}-y\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\leq\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)\leq\lambda_{\max}(H_{\Phi}(\theta))\bigl\|f_{\theta}(x)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}-y\bigr\|_{2}^{2}. (78)

Combining this bound with (A.8) yields the per-sample inequality

λmin​(HΦ​(θ))​ℛΦ∘​(θ,z)λmax​(Ax)≤ℛΦ​(θ,z)≤λmax​(HΦ​(θ))​ℛΦ∘​(θ,z)λmin​(Ax).\lambda_{\min}(H_{\Phi}(\theta))\frac{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)}{\lambda_{\max}(A_{x})}\leq\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)\leq\lambda_{\max}(H_{\Phi}(\theta))\frac{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)}{\lambda_{\min}(A_{x})}. (79)

Taking expectation with respect to Z∼q^Z\sim\hat{q} (the empirical data distribution) gives

𝔼Z​[λmin​(HΦ​(θ))​‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,Z)‖22λmax​(AX)]≤ℛΦ​(θ,s)≤𝔼Z​[λmax​(HΦ​(θ))​‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,Z)‖22λmin​(AX)],\mathbb{E}_{Z}\!\left[\lambda_{\min}(H_{\Phi}(\theta))\frac{\bigl\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}}{\lambda_{\max}(A_{X})}\right]\leq\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,s)\leq\mathbb{E}_{Z}\!\left[\lambda_{\max}(H_{\Phi}(\theta))\frac{\bigl\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}}{\lambda_{\min}(A_{X})}\right], (80)

where ℛΦ​(θ,s)=𝔼Z​[ℛΦ​(θ,Z)]\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,s)=\mathbb{E}_{Z}[\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)] denotes the empirical risk.

Using the definitions

λmin​(As)\displaystyle\lambda_{\min}(A_{s}) :=min(x,y)∈sλmin(Ax),λmax(As):=max(x,y)∈sλmax(Ax),\displaystyle:=\min_{(x,y)\in s}\lambda_{\min}(A_{x}),\quad\lambda_{\max}(A_{s}):=\max_{(x,y)\in s}\lambda_{\max}(A_{x}), (81)

we arrive at

λmin​(HΦ​(s))λmax​(As)​𝔼Z​‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,Z)‖22≤ℛΦ​(θ,s)≤λmax​(HΦ​(s))λmin​(As)​𝔼Z​‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,Z)‖22,\frac{\lambda_{\min}(H_{\Phi}(s))}{\lambda_{\max}(A_{s})}\mathbb{E}_{Z}\bigl\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\leq\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,s)\leq\frac{\lambda_{\max}(H_{\Phi}(s))}{\lambda_{\min}(A_{s})}\mathbb{E}_{Z}\bigl\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}, (82)

which completes the proof of Theorem 10.

A.4 Proof of Corollary 11

Corollary 28.

Let Z∼q^Z\sim\hat{q}.

  1. 1.

    For the MSE loss with Φ⁡(y)=12​‖y‖22\Phi(y)=\frac{1}{2}\|y\|_{2}^{2},

    𝔼Z​[‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,Z)‖22]2​λmax​(As)≤ℛΦ​(θ,s)≤𝔼Z​[‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,Z)‖22]2​λmin​(As).\frac{\mathbb{E}_{Z}\bigl[\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)\|_{2}^{2}\bigr]}{2\lambda_{\max}(A_{s})}\leq\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,s)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}_{Z}\bigl[\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)\|_{2}^{2}\bigr]}{2\lambda_{\min}(A_{s})}.
  2. 2.

    For the softmax cross entropy loss with Φ⁡(q)=−H⁡(q)\Phi(q)=-H(q) where q∈Δq\in\Delta,

    𝔼Z​[‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,Z)‖22]2​ln⁡2⋅λmax​(As)≤ℛΦ​(θ,s)≤𝔼Z​[‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,Z)‖22]mini⁡pi⋅λmin​(As),\frac{\mathbb{E}_{Z}\bigl[\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)\|_{2}^{2}\bigr]}{2\ln 2\cdot\lambda_{\max}(A_{s})}\leq\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,s)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}_{Z}\bigl[\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)\|_{2}^{2}\bigr]}{\min_{i}p_{i}\cdot\lambda_{\min}(A_{s})},

    where p=fθ​(x)Φ∗∗p=f_{\theta}(x)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*} is the softmax output and yy is a one-hot label.

pf.  Part 1 (MSE). For Φ⁡(y)=12​‖y‖22\Phi(y)=\frac{1}{2}\|y\|_{2}^{2}, we have ∇2Φ​(y)=I\nabla^{2}\Phi(y)=I, so λmin​(HΦ​(θ))=λmax​(HΦ​(θ))=1\lambda_{\min}(H_{\Phi}(\theta))=\lambda_{\max}(H_{\Phi}(\theta))=1. The Fenchel–Young loss reduces to the squared error:

ℛΦ​(θ,z)=dΦ​(y,fθ​(x))=12​‖y−fθ​(x)‖22=12​ℛΦ∘​(θ,z).\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)=d_{\Phi}(y,f_{\theta}(x))=\tfrac{1}{2}\|y-f_{\theta}(x)\|_{2}^{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}^{\circ}(\theta,z).

Substituting λmin​(HΦ)=λmax​(HΦ)=1\lambda_{\min}(H_{\Phi})=\lambda_{\max}(H_{\Phi})=1 into Theorem 10 yields the stated bounds.

Part 2 (cross entropy). Let vv be a vector of dimension kk, where k≤∞k\leq\infty. We have:

‖v‖12\displaystyle\|v\|_{1}^{2} =∑i=1k∑j=1k|v⁡(i)|​|v⁡(j)|\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}|v(i)||v(j)| (83)
≥∑i=1k|v⁡(i)|2\displaystyle\geq\sum_{i=1}^{k}|v(i)|^{2}
=‖v‖22.\displaystyle=\|v\|_{2}^{2}.

Let p=fθ​(x)Φ∗∗:=∇Φ∗​(fθ​(x))p=f_{\theta}(x)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}:=\nabla\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x)), which corresponds to the softmax output when Φ\Phi is the negative Shannon entropy. Thus, applying Lemma 6 and substituting the above norm inequality, we obtain:

dΦ​(y,fθ​(x))\displaystyle d_{\Phi}(y,f_{\theta}(x)) =DKL(y∥p)\displaystyle=D_{\text{KL}}(y\|p)
≥12​ln⁡2​‖y−p‖12,\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2\ln 2}\|y-p\|_{1}^{2},
≥12​ln⁡2​‖y−p‖22.\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2\ln 2}\|y-p\|_{2}^{2}.

Using Lemma 5, we further derive:

dΦ​(y,fθ​(x))\displaystyle d_{\Phi}(y,f_{\theta}(x)) =DKL(y∥p)≤1mini⁡pi∥y−p∥22.\displaystyle=D_{\text{KL}}(y\|p)\leq\frac{1}{\min_{i}p_{i}}\|y-p\|_{2}^{2}.

Combining the upper and lower bounds of dΦ​(y,fθ​(x))d_{\Phi}(y,f_{\theta}(x)), we have:

12​ln⁡2​‖y−p‖22≤dΦ​(y,fθ​(x))≤1mini⁡pi​‖y−p‖22.\frac{1}{2\ln 2}\|y-p\|_{2}^{2}\leq d_{\Phi}(y,f_{\theta}(x))\leq\frac{1}{\min_{i}p_{i}}\|y-p\|_{2}^{2}.

Therefore, we can replace λmin​(HΦ​(θ))\lambda_{\min}(H_{\Phi}(\theta)) and λmax​(HΦ​(θ))\lambda_{\max}(H_{\Phi}(\theta)) in Theorem 10 with mini⁡pi\min_{i}p_{i} and 2​ln⁡22\ln 2, respectively, yielding

𝔼Z​[‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,Z)‖22]2​ln⁡2⋅λmax​(As)≤ℛΦ​(θ,s)≤𝔼Z​[‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,Z)‖22]mini⁡pi⋅λmin​(As).\frac{\mathbb{E}_{Z}\bigl[\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)\|_{2}^{2}\bigr]}{2\ln 2\cdot\lambda_{\max}(A_{s})}\leq\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,s)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}_{Z}\bigl[\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)\|_{2}^{2}\bigr]}{\min_{i}p_{i}\cdot\lambda_{\min}(A_{s})}.

A.5 Proof of Theorem 12

Theorem 29.

Let n=|s|n=|s| denote the full dataset size, m=|sk|m=|s_{k}| denote the mini-batch size, and L=maxθ,z∈s⁡λmax​(∇θ2dΦ​(y,fθ​(x)))L=\max_{\theta,z\in s}\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^{2}_{\theta}d_{\Phi}(y,f_{\theta}(x))) denote the Lipschitz constant of the gradient. Applying mini-batch SGD as defined in Equation 44 with the optimal learning rate α=1/(2​L)\alpha=1/(2L) yields:

  1. 1.

    The expected squared batch gradient norm converges to a neighborhood around zero:

    𝔼​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22≤ε2+4​L​(n−m)m​M\mathbb{E}\left\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\right\|_{2}^{2}\leq\varepsilon^{2}+\frac{4L(n-m)}{m}M

    in 𝒪⁡(ε−2)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) iterations for any target precision ε>0\varepsilon>0.

  2. 2.

    For single-sample batches (m=1m=1, vanilla SGD), the gradient energy converges to:

    𝔼Z​‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,Z)‖22≤ε2+4​L​(n−1)​M\mathbb{E}_{Z}\left\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)\right\|_{2}^{2}\leq\varepsilon^{2}+4L(n-1)M

    in 𝒪⁡(ε−2)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) iterations.

pf.  For any batch sks_{k}, after parameter update using ∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k}), the following inequality holds:

ℛΦ​(θk+1,s∖sk)−ℛΦ​(θk,s∖sk)≤M.\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s\setminus s_{k})-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s\setminus s_{k})\leq M.

For the full empirical risk ℛΦ​(θk+1,s)\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s), we decompose the update as:

ℛΦ​(θk+1,s)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s) −ℛΦ​(θk,s)=n−mn​(ℛΦ​(θk+1,s∖sk)−ℛΦ​(θk,s∖sk))\displaystyle-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s)=\frac{n-m}{n}\big(\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s\setminus s_{k})-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s\setminus s_{k})\big)
+mn​(ℛΦ​(θk+1,sk)−ℛΦ​(θk,sk))\displaystyle+\frac{m}{n}\big(\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s_{k})-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\big)
≤n−mn​M+mn​(ℛΦ​(θk+1,sk)−ℛΦ​(θk,sk)).\displaystyle\leq\frac{n-m}{n}M+\frac{m}{n}\big(\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s_{k})-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\big).

For mini-batch SGD with batch size mm, the mean value theorem implies the existence of ξk=t​θk+(1−t)​θk+1\xi_{k}=t\theta_{k}+(1-t)\theta_{k+1} (where t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]) such that:

ℛΦ​(θk+1,sk)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s_{k}) −ℛΦ​(θk,sk)=∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)​(θk+1−θk)\displaystyle-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})=\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})(\theta_{k+1}-\theta_{k})
+(θk+1−θk)⊤​∇θ2ℛΦ​(ξk,sk)​(θk+1−θk)\displaystyle+(\theta_{k+1}-\theta_{k})^{\top}\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\xi_{k},s_{k})(\theta_{k+1}-\theta_{k})
=−α​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22+α2​∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)​∇θ2ℛΦ​(ξk,sk)​∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)⊤.\displaystyle=-\alpha\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\|_{2}^{2}+\alpha^{2}\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\xi_{k},s_{k})\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})^{\top}.

By definition, L=maxθ,z∈s⁡λmax​(∇θ2dΦ​(y,fθ​(x)))=maxθ,z∈s⁡λmax​(∇θ2ℛΦ​(θ,z))L=\max_{\theta,z\in s}\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^{2}_{\theta}d_{\Phi}(y,f_{\theta}(x)))=\max_{\theta,z\in s}\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)). Applying Courant–Fischer min-max theorem, we derive:

ℛΦ​(θk+1,sk)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s_{k}) −ℛΦ​(θk,sk)\displaystyle-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})
≤−α​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22+α2​L​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22\displaystyle\leq-\alpha\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\|_{2}^{2}+\alpha^{2}L\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\|_{2}^{2}
=(α2​L−α)​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22\displaystyle=(\alpha^{2}L-\alpha)\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\|_{2}^{2}
=L⁡(α2−αL+14​L2−14​L2)​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22\displaystyle=L\left(\alpha^{2}-\frac{\alpha}{L}+\frac{1}{4L^{2}}-\frac{1}{4L^{2}}\right)\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\|_{2}^{2}
=L⁡[(α−12​L)2−14​L2]​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22.\displaystyle=L\left[\left(\alpha-\frac{1}{2L}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{4L^{2}}\right]\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\|_{2}^{2}.

This inequality holds for any learning rate α\alpha. Setting the optimal learning rate α=12​L\alpha=\frac{1}{2L} minimizes the upper bound, yielding:

ℛΦ​(θk+1,sk)−ℛΦ​(θk,sk)≤−14​L​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22.\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s_{k})-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\leq-\frac{1}{4L}\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\|_{2}^{2}.

Substituting this result into the full risk update inequality and taking the expectation over random batches sks_{k} on both sides gives:

𝔼sk​[ℛΦ​(θk+1,s)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s_{k}}[\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s)] −ℛΦ​(θk,s)≤n−mn​M+mn​𝔼sk​(ℛΦ​(θk+1,sk)−ℛΦ​(θk,sk))\displaystyle-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s)\leq\frac{n-m}{n}M+\frac{m}{n}\mathbb{E}_{s_{k}}\big(\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s_{k})-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\big)
≤n−mn​M−m4​L​n​𝔼sk​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22.\displaystyle\leq\frac{n-m}{n}M-\frac{m}{4Ln}\mathbb{E}_{s_{k}}\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\|_{2}^{2}.

Rearranging terms to isolate the expected batch gradient norm:

𝔼sk​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22≤4​L​nm​𝔼sk​[ℛΦ​(θk,s)−ℛΦ​(θk+1,s)]+4​L​(n−m)m​M.\mathbb{E}_{s_{k}}\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\|_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{4Ln}{m}\mathbb{E}_{s_{k}}[\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s)-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s)]+\frac{4L(n-m)}{m}M.

We now sum this inequality over iterations k=0,1,…,T−1k=0,1,\ldots,T-1 and take the expectation (denoted by 𝔼\mathbb{E}, assuming independence across batches sis_{i} and sjs_{j}):

mink=0,…,T−1\displaystyle\min_{k=0,\ldots,T-1} 𝔼​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22≤1T​∑k=0T−1𝔼​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\|_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\|_{2}^{2}
≤1T​∑k=0T−14​L​nm​𝔼​[ℛΦ​(θk,s)−ℛΦ​(θk+1,s)]+4​L​(n−m)m​M\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\frac{4Ln}{m}\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s)-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k+1},s)]+\frac{4L(n-m)}{m}M
≤4​L​nm​T​(ℛΦ​(θ0,s)−minθ⁡ℛΦ​(θ,s))+4​L​(n−m)m​M\displaystyle\leq\frac{4Ln}{mT}\big(\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{0},s)-\min_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,s)\big)+\frac{4L(n-m)}{m}M
≤4​L​nm​T​ℛΦ​(θ0,s)+4​L​(n−m)m​M.\displaystyle\leq\frac{4Ln}{mT}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{0},s)+\frac{4L(n-m)}{m}M.

To satisfy the convergence condition 𝔼​‖∇θℛΦ​(θk,sk)‖22≤ε2+4​L​(n−m)m​M\mathbb{E}\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{k},s_{k})\|_{2}^{2}\leq\varepsilon^{2}+\frac{4L(n-m)}{m}M, we require:

4​L​nm​T​ℛΦ​(θ0,s)≤ε2.\frac{4Ln}{mT}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{0},s)\leq\varepsilon^{2}.

Solving for the number of iterations TT:

T\displaystyle T ≥4​L​n​ℛΦ​(θ0,s)m​ε2\displaystyle\geq\frac{4Ln\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta_{0},s)}{m\varepsilon^{2}}
=𝒪⁡(ε−2).\displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}).

This confirms that the iteration complexity scales as 𝒪⁡(ε−2)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) to achieve the desired accuracy.

For the special case of m=1m=1 (single-sample SGD), the convergence condition

𝔼Z​‖∇θℛΦ​(θ,Z)‖22≤ε2+4​L​(n−1)​M\mathbb{E}_{Z}\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,Z)\|_{2}^{2}\leq\varepsilon^{2}+4L(n-1)M

follows directly, with the same iteration complexity of 𝒪⁡(ε−2)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}).

A.6 Proof of Theorem 14

Theorem 30.

Suppose the model has converged to the population optimal prediction, such that the conjugate dual output matches the conditional expectation of the target:

𝔼Y|x​[Y]=fθ​(x)Φ∗∗.\mathbb{E}_{Y|x}[Y]=f_{\theta}(x)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}.

Under this condition, the maximum eigenvalue of the per-sample loss Hessian HzH_{z} satisfies the two-sided bound:

λmin​(Gx)​λmax​(Ax)≤λmax​(Hz)≤λmax​(Gx)​λmax​(Ax),\lambda_{\min}(G_{x})\lambda_{\max}(A_{x})\leq\lambda_{\max}(H_{z})\leq\lambda_{\max}(G_{x})\lambda_{\max}(A_{x}),

where Gx=∇f2Φ∗​(fθ​(x))G_{x}=\nabla^{2}_{f}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x)).

pf.  By definition, the Hessian of the expected loss with respect to the parameters is given by

Hz=∇θ2𝔼Y|x​[dΦ​(Y,fθ​(x))].H_{z}=\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{Y|x}\left[d_{\Phi}(Y,f_{\theta}(x))\right].

Expanding this using the properties of Bregman divergences, we obtain

Hz=∇θfθ​(x)⊤​Gx​∇θfθ​(x)+∇θ2fθ​(x)​(𝔼Y|x​[Y]−fθ​(x)Φ∗∗),H_{z}=\nabla_{\theta}f_{\theta}(x)^{\top}G_{x}\nabla_{\theta}f_{\theta}(x)+\nabla_{\theta}^{2}f_{\theta}(x)\left(\mathbb{E}_{Y|x}[Y]-f_{\theta}(x)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right),

where Gx=∇f2Φ∗​(fθ​(x))G_{x}=\nabla^{2}_{f}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x)) is the Hessian of the convex conjugate Φ∗\Phi^{*} evaluated at fθ​(x)f_{\theta}(x).

After training, the model satisfies the condition

𝔼Y|x​[Y]=fθ​(x)Φ∗∗,\mathbb{E}_{Y|x}[Y]=f_{\theta}(x)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*},

which implies that the second term in the Hessian expansion vanishes. Therefore,

Hz=∇θfθ​(x)⊤​Gx​∇θfθ​(x).H_{z}=\nabla_{\theta}f_{\theta}(x)^{\top}G_{x}\nabla_{\theta}f_{\theta}(x). (84)

Since Φ∗\Phi^{*} is strictly convex, GxG_{x} is positive definite. Applying the Courant–Fischer min-max theorem to this matrix product, we obtain the eigenvalue bound:

λmin​(Gx)​λmax​(Ax)≤λmax​(Hz)≤λmax​(Gx)​λmax​(Ax).\lambda_{\min}(G_{x})\lambda_{\max}(A_{x})\leq\lambda_{\max}(H_{z})\leq\lambda_{\max}(G_{x})\lambda_{\max}(A_{x}).

This completes the proof.

A.7 Proof of Theorem 17

Theorem 31.

In the conjugate learning framework, the empirical risk satisfies the following bounds:

γΦ​(θ)≥ℛΦ​(θ,s)≥EntΦ​(Y′|X′),\displaystyle\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)\geq\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,s)\geq\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(Y^{\prime}|X^{\prime}),

where (X′,Y′)∼q^(X^{\prime},Y^{\prime})\sim\hat{q}. The lower bound is achieved if and only if fθ​(X′)=(Y¯′|X′)Φ∗f_{\theta}(X^{\prime})=(\bar{Y}^{\prime}|X^{\prime})_{\Phi}^{*}.

pf.

Let W=fθ​(X′)Φ∗∗W=f_{\theta}(X^{\prime})_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}. We expand the sum of the generalized conditional entropy as follows:

EntΦ​(Y′|X′)+𝔼X′​dΦ​((Y¯′|X′),fθ​(X′))\displaystyle\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(Y^{\prime}|X^{\prime})+\mathbb{E}_{X^{\prime}}d_{\Phi}((\bar{Y}^{\prime}|X^{\prime}),f_{\theta}(X^{\prime}))
=EntΦ​(Y′|X′)+𝔼X′​BΦ​((Y¯′|X′),W)\displaystyle=\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(Y^{\prime}|X^{\prime})+\mathbb{E}_{X^{\prime}}B_{\Phi}((\bar{Y}^{\prime}|X^{\prime}),W)
=∑x∈𝒳′,y∈𝒴′q⁡(x,y)​[Φ⁡(y)−Φ⁡(Y¯′|x)+Φ⁡(Y¯′|x)−Φ⁡(w)−wΦ∗​((Y¯′|x)−w)]\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}^{\prime},\,y\in\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}}q(x,y)\Big[\Phi(y)-\Phi(\bar{Y}^{\prime}|x)+\Phi(\bar{Y}^{\prime}|x)-\Phi(w)-w_{\Phi}^{*}\big((\bar{Y}^{\prime}|x)-w\big)\Big]
=∑x∈𝒳′,y∈𝒴′q⁡(x,y)​[Φ⁡(y)−Φ⁡(w)−wΦ∗​((Y¯′|x)−w)]\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}^{\prime},\,y\in\mathcal{Y}^{\prime}}q(x,y)\Big[\Phi(y)-\Phi(w)-w_{\Phi}^{*}\big((\bar{Y}^{\prime}|x)-w\big)\Big]
=ℛΦ​(θ,s).\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,s).

Since BΦ​(Y¯′|x′,w)≥0B_{\Phi}(\bar{Y}^{\prime}|x^{\prime},w)\geq 0 for all x′x^{\prime} and ww, we have

ℛΦ​(θ,s)≥EntΦ​(Y′|X′),\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,s)\geq\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(Y^{\prime}|X^{\prime}),

with equality if and only if 𝔼X′​BΦ​((Y¯′|X′),W)=0\mathbb{E}_{X^{\prime}}B_{\Phi}((\bar{Y}^{\prime}|X^{\prime}),W)=0. This condition holds exactly when W=Y¯′|X′W=\bar{Y}^{\prime}|X^{\prime}, which is equivalent to fθ​(X′)=(Y¯′|X′)Φ∗f_{\theta}(X^{\prime})=(\bar{Y}^{\prime}|X^{\prime})_{\Phi}^{*}.

For the upper bound, since γΦ​(θ)\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta) denotes the maximum value of dΦ​(y,fθ​(x))d_{\Phi}(y,f_{\theta}(x)) over all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, we directly obtain

ℛΦ​(θ,s)≤γΦ​(θ).\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,s)\leq\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta).

Combining the lower and upper bound results completes the proof.

A.8 Proof of Theorem 20

Theorem 32.

The deterministic generalization error is bounded as follows. If ℛΦ​(θ,q)≥ℛΦ​(θ,q^)\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,q)\geq\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,\hat{q}), then

gen⁡(fθ,sn)≤γΦ​(θ)−EntΦ​(Y′|X′)−ℒΦ​(Y′|fθ​(X′)).\mathrm{gen}(f_{\theta},s^{n})\leq\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)-\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(Y^{\prime}|X^{\prime})-\mathcal{L}_{\Phi}(Y^{\prime}|f_{\theta}(X^{\prime})).

If ℛΦ​(θ,q)<ℛΦ​(θ,q^)\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,q)<\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,\hat{q}), then

gen⁡(fθ,sn)≤γΦ​(θ)−EntΦ​(Y|X)−ℒΦ​(Y|fθ​(X)).\mathrm{gen}(f_{\theta},s^{n})\leq\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)-\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(Y|X)-\mathcal{L}_{\Phi}(Y|f_{\theta}(X)).

pf.  Let W=fθ​(X)Φ∗∗=g⁡(X)W=f_{\theta}(X)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}=g(X) and W′=fθ​(X′)Φ∗∗=g⁡(X′)W^{\prime}=f_{\theta}(X^{\prime})_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}=g(X^{\prime}). Define the partition of the input space 𝒳\mathcal{X} induced by the function g:𝒳→𝒲g:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{W} as follows: for each wi∈𝒲w_{i}\in\mathcal{W}, let

𝒳i={x∈𝒳|g⁡(x)=wi}.\mathcal{X}_{i}=\{x\in\mathcal{X}|g(x)=w_{i}\}.

Let q⁡(wi)=∑x∈𝒳iq⁡(x)q(w_{i})=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i}}q(x) denote the marginal probability (or weight) of wiw_{i}. For each x∈𝒳ix\in\mathcal{X}_{i}, define the normalized weight

w⁡(x)=q⁡(x)q⁡(wi),w(x)=\frac{q(x)}{q(w_{i})},

so that ∑x∈𝒳iw⁡(x)=1\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i}}w(x)=1. Then, the conditional expectation of Y¯\bar{Y} given wiw_{i} can be expressed as a weighted average:

Y¯|wi=∑x∈𝒳iw⁡(x)​Y¯|x.\bar{Y}|w_{i}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i}}w(x)\bar{Y}|x.

Now, consider the deviation of Y¯|x\bar{Y}|x from Y¯|wi\bar{Y}|w_{i} within 𝒳i\mathcal{X}_{i}:

∑x∈𝒳iq⁡(x)​(Y¯​|x−Y¯|​wi)\displaystyle\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i}}q(x)(\bar{Y}|x-\bar{Y}|w_{i}) =∑x∈𝒳iq⁡(x)​Y¯​|x−q⁡(wi)​Y¯|​wi\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i}}q(x)\bar{Y}|x-q(w_{i})\bar{Y}|w_{i}
=q⁡(wi)​(∑x∈𝒳iw⁡(x)​Y¯​|x−Y¯|​wi)\displaystyle=q(w_{i})\left(\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i}}w(x)\bar{Y}|x-\bar{Y}|w_{i}\right)
=0.\displaystyle=0.

Since this holds for each wiw_{i}, and W=g⁡(X)W=g(X), it follows that for function ∇Φ​(W)\nabla\Phi(W),

𝔼X[∇Φ(W)⊤(Y¯|X−Y¯|W)]=0.\mathbb{E}_{X}\left[\nabla\Phi(W)^{\top}(\bar{Y}|X-\bar{Y}|W)\right]=0.

This orthogonality condition plays a key role in the following generalized conditional entropy analysis. Now, it follows that:

EntΦ​(Y¯|X)\displaystyle\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(\bar{Y}|X) −EntΦ​(Y¯|W)=𝔼X​[Φ⁡(Y¯|X)−Φ⁡(Y¯)]−𝔼W​[Φ⁡(Y¯|W)−Φ⁡(Y¯)]\displaystyle-\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(\bar{Y}|W)=\mathbb{E}_{X}\left[\Phi(\bar{Y}|X)-\Phi(\bar{Y})\right]-\mathbb{E}_{W}\left[\Phi(\bar{Y}|W)-\Phi(\bar{Y})\right]
=𝔼X​[Φ⁡(Y¯|X)−Φ⁡(Y¯|W)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{X}\left[\Phi(\bar{Y}|X)-\Phi(\bar{Y}|W)\right]
=𝔼X[Φ(Y¯|X)−Φ(Y¯|W)]−𝔼X[∇Φ(W)⊤(Y¯|X−Y¯|W)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{X}\left[\Phi(\bar{Y}|X)-\Phi(\bar{Y}|W)\right]-\mathbb{E}_{X}\left[\nabla\Phi(W)^{\top}(\bar{Y}|X-\bar{Y}|W)\right]
=𝔼X[BΦ(Y¯|X,Y¯|W)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{X}\big[B_{\Phi}(\bar{Y}|X,\,\bar{Y}|W)\big]
=ℒΦ​(Y|fθ​(X)).\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\Phi}(Y|f_{\theta}(X)).

This establishes the identity:

EntΦ​(Y¯|X)−EntΦ​(Y¯|W)=ℒΦ​(Y|fθ​(X)),\displaystyle\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(\bar{Y}|X)-\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(\bar{Y}|W)=\mathcal{L}_{\Phi}(Y|f_{\theta}(X)), (85)
EntΦ​(Y¯′|X′)−EntΦ​(Y¯′|W′)=ℒΦ​(Y′|fθ​(X′)).\displaystyle\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(\bar{Y}^{\prime}|X^{\prime})-\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(\bar{Y}^{\prime}|W^{\prime})=\mathcal{L}_{\Phi}(Y^{\prime}|f_{\theta}(X^{\prime})).

By Theorem 17, we have

γΦ​(θ)≥ℛΦ​(θ,q)≥EntΦ​(Y|W),\displaystyle\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)\geq\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,q)\geq\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(Y|W),
γΦ​(θ)≥ℛΦ​(θ,q^)≥EntΦ​(Y′|W′).\displaystyle\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)\geq\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,\hat{q})\geq\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(Y^{\prime}|W^{\prime}).

If ℛΦ​(θ,q)≥ℛΦ​(θ,q^)\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,q)\geq\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,\hat{q}), then subtracting the lower bound of ℛΦ​(θ,q^)\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,\hat{q}) from ℛΦ​(θ,q)\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,q) yields

gen⁡(fθ,sn)\displaystyle\mathrm{gen}(f_{\theta},s^{n}) =ℛΦ​(θ,q)−ℛΦ​(θ,q^)\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,q)-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,\hat{q})
≤γΦ​(θ)−EntΦ​(Y′|W′)\displaystyle\leq\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)-\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(Y^{\prime}|W^{\prime})
=γΦ​(θ)−EntΦ​(Y′|X′)−ℒΦ​(Y′|fθ​(X′))\displaystyle=\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)-\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(Y^{\prime}|X^{\prime})-\mathcal{L}_{\Phi}(Y^{\prime}|f_{\theta}(X^{\prime}))

Similarly, if ℛΦ​(θ,q)<ℛΦ​(θ,q^)\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,q)<\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,\hat{q}), we have

gen⁡(fθ,sn)\displaystyle\mathrm{gen}(f_{\theta},s^{n}) =ℛΦ​(θ,q^)−ℛΦ​(θ,q)\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,\hat{q})-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,q)
≤γΦ​(θ)−EntΦ​(Y|X)−ℒΦ​(Y|fθ​(X)).\displaystyle\leq\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)-\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(Y|X)-\mathcal{L}_{\Phi}(Y|f_{\theta}(X)).

A.9 Proof of Theorem 22

Theorem 33.

Assume training samples sns^{n} are drawn i.i.d. from the true joint distribution q𝒵q_{\mathcal{Z}} over the feature-label space 𝒵=𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{Z}=\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, and the label space 𝒴\mathcal{Y} has finite cardinality (|𝒴|<∞|\mathcal{Y}|<\infty). For any target generalization error threshold ε>0\varepsilon>0, the probability that the generalization error exceeds ε\varepsilon is upper bounded by:

Pr⁡(gen⁡(fθ,sn)≥ε)≤(|𝒳|−ℒ⁡(fθ​(X)))​|𝒴|​γΦ​(θ)2​(1−‖q𝒵‖22)4​n​ε2.\Pr\bigl(\mathrm{gen}(f_{\theta},s^{n})\geq\varepsilon\bigr)\leq\frac{(|\mathcal{X}|-\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(X)))|\mathcal{Y}|\,\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)^{2}\bigl(1-\|q_{\mathcal{Z}}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr)}{4n\varepsilon^{2}}.

Here, ℒ⁡(fθ​(X))=|𝒳|−|fθ​(𝒳)|\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(X))=|\mathcal{X}|-|f_{\theta}(\mathcal{X})| denotes the absolute information loss and n=|sn|n=|s^{n}| is the sample size.

pf.  Since ℛΦ​(θ,z):𝒵→[0,γΦ​(θ)]\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,z):\mathcal{Z}\to[0,\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)] , by the definitions of expected and empirical risk, we have

gen⁡(fθ,sn)\displaystyle\mathrm{gen}(f_{\theta},s^{n}) =|ℛΦ​(θ,q)−ℛΦ​(θ,q^)|\displaystyle=\bigl|\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,q)-\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,\hat{q})\bigr| (86)
=|∑z∈𝒵(q𝒵​(z)−q^𝒵​(z))​ℛΦ​(θ,z)|\displaystyle=\left|\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\bigl(q_{\mathcal{Z}}(z)-\hat{q}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z)\bigr)\,\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)\right|
=|∑z∈𝒵(q𝒵​(z)−q^𝒵​(z))​(ℛΦ​(θ,z)−γΦ​(θ)2)|,\displaystyle=\left|\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\bigl(q_{\mathcal{Z}}(z)-\hat{q}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z)\bigr)\left(\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)-\tfrac{\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)}{2}\right)\right|,

where the last equality follows because ∑z(q𝒵​(z)−q^𝒵​(z))=0\sum_{z}(q_{\mathcal{Z}}(z)-\hat{q}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z))=0 .

Applying the triangle inequality and noting that |ℛΦ​(θ,z)−γΦ​(θ)2|≤γΦ​(θ)2|\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(\theta,z)-\tfrac{\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)}{2}|\leq\tfrac{\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)}{2} , we obtain

gen⁡(fθ,sn)≤γΦ​(θ)2​‖q𝒵−q^𝒵‖1.\mathrm{gen}(f_{\theta},s^{n})\leq\frac{\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)}{2}\,\|q_{\mathcal{Z}}-\hat{q}_{\mathcal{Z}}\|_{1}.

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

‖q𝒵−q^𝒵‖1=∑z∈𝒵|q𝒵​(z)−q^𝒵​(z)|≤|𝒵|​‖q𝒵−q^𝒵‖2.\|q_{\mathcal{Z}}-\hat{q}_{\mathcal{Z}}\|_{1}=\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}|q_{\mathcal{Z}}(z)-\hat{q}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z)|\leq\sqrt{|\mathcal{Z}|}\,\|q_{\mathcal{Z}}-\hat{q}_{\mathcal{Z}}\|_{2}.

Substituting this bound yields

gen⁡(fθ,sn)≤|𝒵|​γΦ​(θ)2​‖q𝒵−q^𝒵‖2.\mathrm{gen}(f_{\theta},s^{n})\leq\frac{\sqrt{|\mathcal{Z}|}\,\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)}{2}\,\|q_{\mathcal{Z}}-\hat{q}_{\mathcal{Z}}\|_{2}.

Let Q^𝒵n\hat{Q}_{\mathcal{Z}}^{n} denote the empirical distribution induced by an i.i.d. sample sn∼q𝒵⊗ns^{n}\sim q_{\mathcal{Z}}^{\otimes n} . Since sns^{n} is random, Q^𝒵n\hat{Q}_{\mathcal{Z}}^{n} is a random variable satisfying 𝔼sn​[Q^𝒵n]=q𝒵\mathbb{E}_{s^{n}}[\hat{Q}_{\mathcal{Z}}^{n}]=q_{\mathcal{Z}} .

Applying Markov’s inequality to the squared generalization error gives

Pr⁡(gen⁡(fθ,sn)≥ε)≤𝔼⁡[gen​(fθ,sn)2]ε2≤|𝒵|​γΦ​(θ)24​ε2​𝔼​[‖q𝒵−Q^𝒵n‖22].\Pr\bigl(\mathrm{gen}(f_{\theta},s^{n})\geq\varepsilon\bigr)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{gen}(f_{\theta},s^{n})^{2}\big]}{\varepsilon^{2}}\leq\frac{|\mathcal{Z}|\,\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)^{2}}{4\varepsilon^{2}}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\|q_{\mathcal{Z}}-\hat{Q}_{\mathcal{Z}}^{n}\|_{2}^{2}\big].

Because the samples are i.i.d., the MSE loss satisfies

𝔼⁡[‖q𝒵−Q^𝒵n‖22]=1n​𝔼Z∼q𝒵​[‖𝟏Z−q𝒵‖22]=1−‖q𝒵‖22n.\mathbb{E}\big[\|q_{\mathcal{Z}}-\hat{Q}_{\mathcal{Z}}^{n}\|_{2}^{2}\big]=\frac{1}{n}\,\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim q_{\mathcal{Z}}}\big[\|\mathbf{1}_{Z}-q_{\mathcal{Z}}\|_{2}^{2}\big]=\frac{1-\|q_{\mathcal{Z}}\|_{2}^{2}}{n}.

Recall that the absolute information loss is defined as ℒ⁡(fθ​(X))=|𝒳|−|𝒲g|\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(X))=|\mathcal{X}|-|\mathcal{W}_{g}| , where 𝒲g\mathcal{W}_{g} is the image of the mapping g=fθg=f_{\theta} . Since the effective support size of the representation is |𝒲g|=|𝒳|−ℒ⁡(fθ​(X))|\mathcal{W}_{g}|=|\mathcal{X}|-\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(X)) , and each input maps to a label in 𝒴\mathcal{Y} , the relevant cardinality in the generalization bound is |𝒲g|⋅|𝒴|=(|𝒳|−ℒ⁡(fθ​(X)))​|𝒴||\mathcal{W}_{g}|\cdot|\mathcal{Y}|=(|\mathcal{X}|-\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(X)))|\mathcal{Y}| , which replaces |𝒵|=|𝒳|​|𝒴||\mathcal{Z}|=|\mathcal{X}||\mathcal{Y}| .

Thus, substituting this refined cardinality into the bound yields

Pr⁡(gen⁡(fθ,sn)≥ε)≤(|𝒳|−ℒ⁡(fθ​(X)))​|𝒴|​γΦ​(θ)2​(1−‖q𝒵‖22)4​n​ε2,\Pr\bigl(\mathrm{gen}(f_{\theta},s^{n})\geq\varepsilon\bigr)\leq\frac{\bigl(|\mathcal{X}|-\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(X))\bigr)|\mathcal{Y}|\,\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)^{2}\bigl(1-\|q_{\mathcal{Z}}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr)}{4n\varepsilon^{2}},

which completes the proof.

A.10 Proof of Lemma 23

Lemma 34.

Let Θϵ′={θ∈Θ∣‖θ‖22≤ϵ}\Theta^{\prime}_{\epsilon}=\left\{\theta\in\Theta\mid\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}\leq\epsilon\right\} denote a closed ball of radius ϵ\sqrt{\epsilon} around the zero parameter vector in the parameter space Θ\Theta. Assume:

  1. 1.

    For all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, the zero-parameter model outputs the zero vector: f𝟎​(x)=𝟎f_{\mathbf{0}}(x)=\mathbf{0};

  2. 2.

    The zero output minimizes the conjugate function: Φ∗​(𝟎)=minθ∈Θ⁡Φ∗​(fθ​(x))\Phi^{*}(\mathbf{0})=\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x)) for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}.

Then there exist positive constants aa, bb, and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that for all θ∈Θϵ′\theta\in\Theta^{\prime}_{\epsilon} and all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, the parameter norm controls the conjugate function as follows:

a​‖θ‖22≤Φ∗​(fθ​(x))−Φ∗​(𝟎)≤b​‖θ‖22.a\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}\leq\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x))-\Phi^{*}(\mathbf{0})\leq b\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}.

pf.  Since θ=𝟎\theta=\mathbf{0} is the minimizer of Φ∗​(fθ​(x))\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x)) over θ\theta, the first and second-order optimality conditions hold for all θ∈Θϵ′\theta\in\Theta^{\prime}_{\epsilon}:

∇θΦ∗​(fθ​(x))|θ=𝟎\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x))\bigg|_{\theta=\mathbf{0}} =𝟎,\displaystyle=\mathbf{0}, (87)
∇θ2Φ∗​(fθ​(x))\displaystyle\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x)) ⪰0,\displaystyle\succeq 0,
λmax​(∇θ2Φ∗​(fθ​(x)))\displaystyle\lambda_{\max}\left(\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x))\right) ≥λmin​(∇θ2Φ∗​(fθ​(x)))≥0,\displaystyle\geq\lambda_{\min}\left(\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x))\right)\geq 0,

where λmax​(⋅)\lambda_{\max}(\cdot) and λmin​(⋅)\lambda_{\min}(\cdot) denote the maximum and minimum eigenvalues of a matrix, respectively.

By Taylor’s theorem (second-order mean value theorem for multivariate functions) applied to Φ∗​(fθ​(x))\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x)) around θ=𝟎\theta=\mathbf{0}, there exists θ′=α​θ\theta^{\prime}=\alpha\theta for some α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] (i.e., θ′\theta^{\prime} lies on the line segment between 𝟎\mathbf{0} and θ\theta) such that:

Φ∗​(fθ​(x))=Φ∗​(f𝟎​(x))+θ⊤​∇θ2Φ∗​(fθ′​(x))​θ.\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x))=\Phi^{*}(f_{\mathbf{0}}(x))+\theta^{\top}\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta^{\prime}}(x))\theta. (88)

Given f𝟎=𝟎f_{\mathbf{0}}=\mathbf{0}, this simplifies to:

Φ∗​(fθ​(x))−Φ∗​(𝟎)=θ⊤​∇θ2Φ∗​(fθ′​(x))​θ.\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x))-\Phi^{*}(\mathbf{0})=\theta^{\top}\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta^{\prime}}(x))\theta. (89)

By the Courant–Fischer min-max theorem (which characterizes the extremal eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix), for any vector θ\theta and symmetric positive semi-definite matrix AA, we have:

λmin​(A)​‖θ‖22≤θ⊤​A​θ≤λmax​(A)​‖θ‖22.\lambda_{\min}(A)\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}\leq\theta^{\top}A\theta\leq\lambda_{\max}(A)\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}.

Applying this to A=∇θ2Φ∗​(fθ′​(x))A=\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta^{\prime}}(x)) (which is positive semi-definite by Equation 87), we obtain:

λmin​(∇θ2Φ∗​(fθ′​(x)))​‖θ‖22\displaystyle\lambda_{\min}\left(\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta^{\prime}}(x))\right)\|\theta\|_{2}^{2} ≤Φ∗​(fθ​(x))−Φ∗​(𝟎)\displaystyle\leq\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x))-\Phi^{*}(\mathbf{0}) (90)
≤λmax​(∇θ2Φ∗​(fθ′​(x)))​‖θ‖22.\displaystyle\leq\lambda_{\max}\left(\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta^{\prime}}(x))\right)\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}.

Define the positive constants aa and bb as the infimum and supremum of the extremal eigenvalues over Θϵ′\Theta^{\prime}_{\epsilon}, respectively:

a\displaystyle a =infθ∈Θϵ′λmin​(∇θ2Φ∗​(fθ′​(x))),\displaystyle=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta^{\prime}_{\epsilon}}\lambda_{\min}\left(\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta^{\prime}}(x))\right), (91)
b\displaystyle b =supθ∈Θϵ′λmax​(∇θ2Φ∗​(fθ′​(x))).\displaystyle=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta^{\prime}_{\epsilon}}\lambda_{\max}\left(\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta^{\prime}}(x))\right).

Since Θϵ′\Theta^{\prime}_{\epsilon} is a compact set (closed and bounded subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space) and the eigenvalue functions are continuous, aa and bb are well-defined positive constants.

Thus, for all θ∈Θϵ′\theta\in\Theta^{\prime}_{\epsilon}, we conclude:

a​‖θ‖22≤Φ∗​(fθ​(x))−Φ∗​(𝟎)≤b​‖θ‖22.a\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}\leq\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x))-\Phi^{*}(\mathbf{0})\leq b\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}.

This completes the proof.

A.11 Proof of Proposition 24

Proposition 35.

In classification tasks, if f𝟎​(x)=𝟎f_{\mathbf{0}}(x)=\mathbf{0} for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and 𝟎Φ∗=u\mathbf{0}_{\Phi^{*}}=u, where uu is the uniform distribution on 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, then reducing ‖θ‖22\|\theta\|_{2}^{2} is equivalent to reducing γΦ​(θ)\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta).

pf.  Let Y′Y^{\prime} be a random variable taking values in the label space 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, such that its conditional distribution given X=xX=x is uniform over 𝒴\mathcal{Y} for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} (i.e., Y′|X=x∼uY^{\prime}|X=x\sim u).

By the definition of the expected Fenchel–Young loss and the properties of uniform distributions, we establish the following tight bounds:

𝔼Y′​[dΦ​(𝟏Y′,(fθ​(x))Φ∗∗)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{Y^{\prime}}\left[d_{\Phi}\left(\mathbf{1}_{Y^{\prime}},\left(f_{\theta}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right)\right] ≤maxy∈𝒴⁡dΦ​(𝟏y,(fθ​(x))Φ∗∗)\displaystyle\leq\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}d_{\Phi}\left(\mathbf{1}_{y},\left(f_{\theta}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right)
≤|𝒴|⋅𝔼Y′​[dΦ​(𝟏Y′,(fθ​(x))Φ∗∗)].\displaystyle\leq|\mathcal{Y}|\cdot\mathbb{E}_{Y^{\prime}}\left[d_{\Phi}\left(\mathbf{1}_{Y^{\prime}},\left(f_{\theta}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right)\right].

Since the expected Fenchel–Young loss can be decomposed as:

𝔼Y′​[dΦ​(𝟏Y′,(fθ​(x))Φ∗∗)]=EntΦ​(Y′)+dΦ​(u,(fθ​(x))Φ∗∗).\mathbb{E}_{Y^{\prime}}\left[d_{\Phi}\left(\mathbf{1}_{Y^{\prime}},\left(f_{\theta}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right)\right]=\mathrm{Ent}_{\Phi}(Y^{\prime})+d_{\Phi}\left(u,\left(f_{\theta}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right).

Thus, minimizing the Fenchel–Young divergence between the uniform distribution and the conjugate dual of the model output (i.e., dΦ​(u,(fθ​(x))Φ∗∗)d_{\Phi}\left(u,\left(f_{\theta}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right)) is equivalent to minimizing 𝔼Y′​[dΦ​(𝟏Y′,(fθ​(x))Φ∗∗)]\mathbb{E}_{Y^{\prime}}\left[d_{\Phi}\left(\mathbf{1}_{Y^{\prime}},\left(f_{\theta}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right)\right]. We also conclude that minimizing dΦ​(u,(fθ​(x))Φ∗∗)d_{\Phi}\left(u,\left(f_{\theta}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right) is equivalent to minimizing maxy∈𝒴⁡dΦ​(𝟏y,(fθ​(x))Φ∗∗)\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}d_{\Phi}\left(\mathbf{1}_{y},\left(f_{\theta}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right).

From Lemma 23, there exist positive constants a,b>0a,b>0 and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that for all θ∈Θϵ′={θ∣‖θ‖22≤ϵ}\theta\in\Theta^{\prime}_{\epsilon}=\left\{\theta\mid\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}\leq\epsilon\right\}, the following equivalence holds:

a​‖θ‖22≤Φ∗​(fθ​(x))−Φ∗​(𝟎)=dΦ​((f𝟎​(x))Φ∗∗,fθ​(x))≤b​‖θ‖22.a\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}\leq\Phi^{*}(f_{\theta}(x))-\Phi^{*}(\mathbf{0})=d_{\Phi}\left(\left(f_{\mathbf{0}}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*},f_{\theta}(x)\right)\leq b\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}.

By the proposition’s assumption that 𝟎Φ∗=u\mathbf{0}_{\Phi^{*}}=u and f𝟎​(x)=𝟎f_{\mathbf{0}}(x)=\mathbf{0} for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, we have (f𝟎​(x))Φ∗∗=u\left(f_{\mathbf{0}}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}=u. Substituting this into the inequality above, we find that minimizing ‖θ‖22\|\theta\|_{2}^{2} (within the neighborhood Θϵ′\Theta^{\prime}_{\epsilon} around θ=𝟎\theta=\mathbf{0}) is equivalent to minimizing dΦ​(u,(fθ​(x))Φ∗∗)d_{\Phi}\left(u,\left(f_{\theta}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right).

Since γΦ​(θ)=max(x,y)∈𝒵⁡dΦ​(𝟏y,(fθ​(x))Φ∗∗)\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)=\max_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{Z}}d_{\Phi}\left(\mathbf{1}_{y},\left(f_{\theta}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right) (by the definition of γΦ​(θ)\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta)), minimizing dΦ​(u,(fθ​(x))Φ∗∗)d_{\Phi}\left(u,\left(f_{\theta}(x)\right)_{\Phi^{*}}^{*}\right) directly reduces the maximum loss value γΦ​(θ)\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta). Combining these results, we conclude that reducing ‖θ‖22\|\theta\|_{2}^{2} (in a neighborhood of θ=𝟎\theta=\mathbf{0}) is equivalent to reducing γΦ​(θ)\gamma_{\Phi}(\theta).

This completes the proof.
